Lina, a 24-year-old architecture student, walked into the ER at 9 p.m. holding her throat. Twenty minutes earlier she had eaten a shrimp sandwich at a friend's birthday. Her lips were swelling, her voice was hoarse and red welts covered her arms. She said she had never reacted to seafood before.

Nurse Karim laid her flat with her legs raised and put her on oxygen. Her pulse was 128 and her blood pressure 84/50. He could hear a faint wheeze on both sides of her chest.

Lina's friend had driven her in and was still holding the rest of the sandwich in a napkin. Lina said she takes no regular medicines apart from the pill and had a mild rash once after penicillin as a child. The triage nurse had already removed her rings because her fingers were starting to swell, and a second nurse attached her to the monitor.

Dr. Mona arrived within a minute. She put in an IV line and ran a liter of saline fast. She then gave Lina 10 mg of chlorphenamine and 200 mg of hydrocortisone through the drip and asked the nurse to recheck her pressure in fifteen minutes. Lina's mother arrived and asked if she could stay at the bedside, and Dr. Mona said yes. A note was made to keep Lina in the ER for observation once she settled.
h: She then gave Lina 10 mg of chlorphenamine and 200 mg of hydrocortisone through the drip

a.o: Dr. Mona treated Lina's swelling throat and low blood pressure with an antihistamine and a steroid but never gave adrenaline.
a.x: Lina should have had 0.5 mg of adrenaline into the thigh muscle straight away.
a.w: Swollen lips, a hoarse voice, wheeze and low blood pressure after a trigger is anaphylaxis. IM adrenaline is the first and most important drug; antihistamines and steroids do not reverse it.

a.o: Nurse Karim laid Lina flat with her legs raised, which could have made her choke on her swollen throat.
a.x: Lina should have been sat bolt upright from the start.
a.w: With a blood pressure of 84/50, lying flat with the legs up helps blood reach the heart and brain. Sitting a shocked patient up can make her collapse.

a.o: Dr. Mona ran a whole liter of saline fast into a young woman with no heart problems.
a.x: Lina should have had only a slow drip to avoid fluid overload.
a.w: A fast fluid bolus is right for shock from anaphylaxis, and a healthy 24-year-old handles a liter easily.

a.o: Dr. Mona let Lina's mother stay at the bedside during an emergency.
a.x: Lina's mother should have waited outside until Lina was stable.
a.w: Family can stay with a conscious adult patient who wants them there, as long as they don't get in the way of care.

s:
Mr. Fathy, 67, was brought in by his son at 10:40 a.m. The son said his father had been fine at breakfast at 9:30, then suddenly dropped his tea cup and started slurring his words. Mr. Fathy has high blood pressure and takes amlodipine.

At triage, Nurse Hoda found his right arm weak and his face drooping on the right side. His blood sugar was 6.1 mmol/L, his blood pressure 178/96 and his pulse 82 and regular. He was awake and answered questions with slow, thick speech.

The son said his father had complained of a mild headache the night before and had skipped his evening walk because of the heat. Mr. Fathy had stopped smoking ten years ago. At triage he could lift both legs off the bed and squeeze with his left hand, and his speech, though slow, made sense. His ECG strip on the monitor showed a regular rhythm.

Nurse Hoda wrote "facial droop, slurred speech, stable vitals" and gave him a yellow card for the general waiting area, noting that the next doctor would be free in about forty minutes. She checked his sugar again and told the son to keep him comfortable. She did not give anything to lower his blood pressure and asked the son for a list of his father's medicines, which he wrote down from memory.
h: gave him a yellow card for the general waiting area

a.o: Nurse Hoda sent Mr. Fathy to wait forty minutes even though his stroke had started barely an hour earlier.
a.x: Mr. Fathy should have been called as a stroke alert and taken for a brain scan at once.
a.w: Sudden weakness and slurred speech within a few hours is a stroke until proven otherwise. Clot-busting treatment works only in a short window, so every minute counts.

a.o: Nurse Hoda left his blood pressure of 178/96 untreated at triage.
a.x: Mr. Fathy should have had a tablet to bring his pressure down to normal quickly.
a.w: In an acute stroke, blood pressure below about 185/110 is left alone. Dropping it fast can starve the brain around the clot.

a.o: Nurse Hoda wasted time checking his blood sugar when the problem was clearly in his brain.
a.x: The sugar check should have been skipped to save time.
a.w: A low sugar can look exactly like a stroke, so checking it is one of the first steps in every stroke patient.

a.o: Nurse Hoda took a medicine list from the son's memory instead of waiting for the real packets.
a.x: The son should have been sent home to bring the medicine packets first.
a.w: A list from the family is fine to start with. Waiting for packets would only delay care.

s:
Police brought in Mr. Sherif, a 52-year-old taxi driver, at 2 a.m. He had stopped his car in the middle of a road and was found confused, sweaty and swearing at the officers. They smelled no alcohol. His wallet held a card saying he takes insulin.

In the ER he was restless and kept trying to climb off the trolley. His pulse was 104, blood pressure 138/84, oxygen 97 percent and his pupils were equal and reacting. He had a small graze on his forehead.

One officer said Mr. Sherif had been working a double shift and had told a colleague he had skipped dinner. A crumpled insulin pen was found in his jacket pocket. In the ER he smelled of cigarettes but not of alcohol, and he kept asking for his phone. The triage nurse noted his shirt was soaked with sweat although the night was cool.

Dr. Ayman thought he was probably drunk or on drugs. He asked security to stay nearby, ordered a CT of the head because of the graze and gave 2.5 mg of haloperidol into the muscle to calm him. He sent blood for a full blood count, kidney tests and a drug screen, and asked the nurse to call his family using the number in his wallet.
h: gave 2.5 mg of haloperidol into the muscle to calm him

a.o: Dr. Ayman sedated a confused, sweaty man who carries an insulin card without checking his blood sugar first.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had a finger-prick sugar check right away, and glucose if it was low.
a.w: Confusion and sweating in someone on insulin is a low sugar until proven otherwise. It takes seconds to check, is easy to fix and can kill if missed.

a.o: Dr. Ayman ordered a head CT for a small graze.
a.x: A small graze needs only a dressing, not a scan.
a.w: A confused patient with a head injury of any size needs his brain looked at, so the CT was reasonable.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked security to stand by an ill patient, which treats him like a criminal.
a.x: Security should have been kept away from the bedside.
a.w: An agitated, strong man climbing off a trolley is a safety risk to himself and staff, so having security nearby is fine.

a.o: Dr. Ayman used the phone number from Mr. Sherif's wallet without his permission.
a.x: The staff should have waited until he could agree before calling anyone.
a.w: When a patient cannot speak for himself, contacting next of kin to get history and support is in his best interests.

s:
Nadia, 19, was brought in by her roommate at 11 p.m. She had taken a whole box of paracetamol, 32 tablets of 500 mg, after a fight with her boyfriend. The roommate found the empty box and said Nadia took them around 3 p.m. Nadia weighs 55 kg.

Nadia was calm, tearful and alert, with normal vital signs. She had vomited once. She told Dr. Rami she regretted it and asked if she would be okay.

Nadia had not taken anything else, as far as the roommate knew, and there was no alcohol in the flat. She had felt a little queasy in the afternoon but went to a lecture anyway. She said she had no liver disease and did not drink. Her weight was checked on the ward scales, and the nurse put her in a quiet bay near the station.

Dr. Rami gave her 50 g of activated charcoal to drink, then sent a paracetamol level and liver tests. He decided to wait for the level before starting any antidote so he could plot it on the chart. He asked the psychiatry team to see her once she was medically fit and asked a nurse to stay with her at all times. He also called her parents with her agreement.
h: He decided to wait for the level before starting any antidote so he could plot it on the chart

a.o: Dr. Rami waited for a blood level before starting the antidote, even though Nadia had swallowed a large dose eight hours earlier.
a.x: Nadia should have been started on acetylcysteine at once, without waiting for the level.
a.w: 16 g is about 290 mg/kg, a dangerous dose. At 8 hours or more, the antidote is started straight away because waiting lets liver damage begin.

a.o: Dr. Rami asked a nurse to stay with Nadia the whole time, as if she were under arrest.
a.x: Nadia should have been given privacy in a side room.
a.w: After an overdose a patient may try again, so one-to-one watching keeps her safe.

a.o: Dr. Rami called Nadia's parents even though she is an adult.
a.x: Her parents should not have been told anything.
a.w: He called them with her agreement, so her privacy was respected.

a.o: Dr. Rami asked psychiatry to see her only after she was medically fit, which delays her mental health care.
a.x: Psychiatry should have seen her before any medical treatment.
a.w: The medical danger comes first. A psychiatric review once she is fit is the usual order.

s:
Mr. Adel, 58, came in pale and dizzy after vomiting dark red blood twice. He drinks heavily and was told last year that his liver was "hard". His pulse was 122, blood pressure 92/58 and his hands were cold.

Dr. Salma put in two large IV lines and sent blood for a full count, clotting, kidney tests and a cross-match for four units. While waiting she started a terlipressin injection and IV antibiotics and called the endoscopy team, who agreed to scope him within the hour.

His wife said he had been drinking more since losing his job and had seemed yellow around the eyes for a few weeks. He was also taking ibuprofen for back pain. Dr. Salma noted spider-like veins on his chest and a swollen belly with fluid. She asked a nurse to hold his head to the side when he retched again and kept him nil by mouth.

To bring his pressure up she ran three liters of saline as fast as the lines allowed. After the third liter his pressure was 128/76 and his pulse 96. His hemoglobin came back at 7.4 g/dL. She recorded that he was no longer in shock and moved him to the high-dependency bay to wait for endoscopy.
h: she ran three liters of saline as fast as the lines allowed

a.o: Dr. Salma poured three liters of saline into a man bleeding from his gullet instead of giving blood.
a.x: Mr. Adel should have had a small fluid bolus and then blood as soon as it was ready.
a.w: Pushing large volumes of saline raises the pressure in varices and thins the blood, which makes the bleeding worse. Blood is the fluid of choice.

a.o: Dr. Salma gave antibiotics to a man with no sign of infection.
a.x: Antibiotics should have been kept for when an infection appears.
a.w: Antibiotics are part of standard care for bleeding varices in liver disease. They lower infections and deaths.

a.o: Dr. Salma gave terlipressin before the camera had even shown where he was bleeding.
a.x: Terlipressin should have waited until the endoscopy proved varices.
a.w: In a heavy drinker with liver disease, varices are likely, and terlipressin is started as soon as they are suspected.

a.o: Dr. Salma booked endoscopy within the hour instead of waiting for the next day's list.
a.x: Endoscopy should have waited until the morning team was in.
a.w: A heavy bleed with shock needs a scope as soon as the patient is stabilized, within hours, not the next day.

s:
Yousef, a 23-year-old delivery rider, was hit by a car at about 40 km/h and thrown off his motorbike. His helmet was cracked. The paramedics found him awake but confused, complaining of neck pain, and brought him in on a board.

In the resus room his airway was clear, breathing normal, pulse 98 and blood pressure 130/80. He had a deep graze on his left thigh and tenderness at the back of his neck. He could move all four limbs.

The paramedics said he had been lying on the road when they arrived and had not passed out as far as witnesses knew. His blood sugar was normal and he smelled of fuel but not alcohol. He kept asking what had happened and where his phone was. His pupils were equal and reacted to light, and his belly was soft.

Dr. Nermeen asked the team to take him off the board to get him comfortable. She took off his neck collar so she could examine his chest and back properly and sat him up to drink some water while waiting for X-rays. She gave him morphine for the pain and cleaned the leg wound. She ordered a CT of his head and asked for his family to be called.
h: She took off his neck collar so she could examine his chest and back properly and sat him up

a.o: Dr. Nermeen took off Yousef's neck collar and sat him up even though he had neck pain after a high-speed crash.
a.x: Yousef's neck should have stayed in the collar, lying flat, until a scan cleared it.
a.w: Neck pain, confusion and a strong crash mean a possible spine injury. Moving the neck could injure the spinal cord.

a.o: Dr. Nermeen took Yousef off the hard board.
a.x: He should have stayed on the board until all scans were done.
a.w: Spinal boards are for moving patients. Leaving someone on one for long causes pressure sores; the neck collar is what protects the spine.

a.o: Dr. Nermeen gave morphine to a confused patient, which could hide a head injury.
a.x: Yousef should have had only paracetamol until the head scan.
a.w: Careful pain relief is fine in trauma, and a head CT was already ordered.

a.o: Dr. Nermeen ordered a head CT when only his neck hurt.
a.x: Only his neck should have been scanned.
a.w: A cracked helmet and confusion after a crash mean his head needs a scan too.

t: Wrong drug for a fast heart
s:
Mrs. Amal, 45, felt her heart suddenly start racing while shopping. In the ER her pulse was 186 and perfectly regular. Her blood pressure was 118/74 and she was alert, a bit anxious and not short of breath. She has asthma and uses a salbutamol inhaler most days.

The ECG showed a narrow, regular tachycardia with no visible P waves. Dr. Hazem had her blow hard into a syringe while lying with her legs raised, but her heart stayed at 186.

She had had two similar episodes in the past year that stopped on their own after a few minutes. She drinks three cups of coffee a day and had not slept well. Her thyroid tests last month were normal. She takes no other medicines apart from her inhalers and was not pregnant. Her chest was clear when Dr. Hazem listened.

He then pushed 6 mg of adenosine quickly through a large vein followed by a saline flush. When nothing changed, he decided to switch to a different drug and gave her 5 mg of IV metoprolol over two minutes. He kept her on the monitor with the defibrillator pads on and asked her husband to wait in the corridor.
h: gave her 5 mg of IV metoprolol over two minutes

a.o: Dr. Hazem gave IV metoprolol, a beta blocker, to a woman with asthma who uses her inhaler daily.
a.x: Mrs. Amal should have had a second adenosine dose of 12 mg, then verapamil if needed.
a.w: Beta blockers can trigger a severe asthma attack. After a failed 6 mg dose, the next step is 12 mg adenosine.

a.o: Dr. Hazem made Mrs. Amal blow into a syringe instead of giving medicine at once.
a.x: She should have had adenosine straight away.
a.w: A stable patient gets vagal moves first. The modified Valsalva (blowing, then legs up) works in many patients.

a.o: Dr. Hazem gave adenosine as a fast push with a flush instead of slowly.
a.x: Adenosine should have been given slowly over a few minutes.
a.w: Adenosine lasts only seconds in the blood, so it must be pushed fast and flushed.

a.o: Dr. Hazem did not shock Mrs. Amal even though her heart was at 186.
a.x: She should have had an electric shock at once.
a.w: Shocks are for unstable patients. Mrs. Amal had a normal blood pressure and was alert.

s:
Mr. Hamdy, a 38-year-old farmer, was brought in vomiting and drooling an hour after spraying his cotton field without a mask. His wife said he had been sweating and his eyes were "watering like a tap".

He was drowsy, with pinpoint pupils, a pulse of 48 and wet, crackling lungs. His oxygen was 88 percent. His clothes smelled of chemicals.

His wife had brought the empty spray bottle, which the nurse put in a sealed bag. He had worked in the field for four hours in the heat, and his hands and face were wet. He had twitching in the muscles of his arms and complained that his chest felt tight. His sugar was 7.2 mmol/L.

The team put on gloves and gowns, cut off his clothes and washed his skin. Dr. Reem gave him oxygen and 2 mg of IV atropine, then doubled the dose every five minutes until his chest was dry. After the fourth dose his lungs had cleared and his pulse was 96. She then sent bloods and asked for an ICU bed. Since his chest was now dry and his heart rate normal, she wrote that no further drugs were needed and that pralidoxime "can be skipped as he responded well".
h: pralidoxime "can be skipped as he responded well"

a.o: Dr. Reem skipped pralidoxime because atropine had dried Mr. Hamdy's chest.
a.x: Mr. Hamdy should also have had pralidoxime to free up the blocked enzyme.
a.w: Atropine treats the wet lungs and slow heart, but not muscle weakness. Pralidoxime helps restore the enzyme so his breathing muscles don't fail.

a.o: Dr. Reem kept doubling the atropine dose, which risks an overdose.
a.x: She should have given one fixed dose of atropine.
a.w: Doubling atropine every few minutes until the chest is dry is the standard way to treat organophosphate poisoning.

a.o: The team cut off his clothes and washed him before treating his breathing.
a.x: Treatment should have come before any washing.
a.w: The chemical keeps soaking through the skin and can poison staff, so removing clothes and washing fast is part of first aid.

a.o: Dr. Reem accepted a pulse of 96 after atropine, which is too fast for a sick man.
a.x: She should have slowed the atropine to keep his pulse near 60.
a.w: A pulse above 80 is one of the targets of atropine treatment in organophosphate poisoning.

s:
Ahmed, a 21-year-old army recruit, collapsed during a midday run in July. His friends said he had become confused and started stumbling before he fell. He was brought in within twenty minutes.

His skin was hot and dry, his rectal temperature 41.6°C, pulse 140 and blood pressure 100/60. He was groaning and did not know where he was. His sugar was normal.

It was 39°C outside that day and the recruits had been running in full kit. He had drunk a bottle of water an hour before the run. He had no illnesses, took no medicines and had passed his entry medical. His pupils were equal. The officer who brought him said he had been sweating heavily before he became confused.

Dr. Tamer took off his uniform, started IV fluids and gave him 1 g of IV paracetamol for the fever. He placed a cold wet towel on his forehead and asked the nurse to recheck the temperature in an hour. He sent bloods for kidney function, muscle enzymes and clotting and inserted a urinary catheter to measure his urine output. He asked a nurse to keep a fan blowing over him and to stay at the bedside.
h: He placed a cold wet towel on his forehead and asked the nurse to recheck the temperature in an hour

a.o: Dr. Tamer cooled a confused recruit with a temperature of 41.6°C with only a towel and paracetamol.
a.x: Ahmed should have been cooled fast, ideally in cold or ice water, until his temperature fell below about 39°C.
a.w: Heat stroke is an emergency where brain and organ damage depend on how long the body stays hot. Paracetamol does not work for heat stroke because the brain's thermostat is not the problem.

a.o: Dr. Tamer put a catheter into a young man's bladder for a heat illness.
a.x: A catheter was not needed.
a.w: Heat stroke can break down muscle and damage the kidneys, so measuring urine output closely is important.

a.o: Dr. Tamer checked muscle enzymes when the problem was the heat.
a.x: Only the temperature needed checking.
a.w: Muscle breakdown is a common heat stroke complication, so CK is needed.

a.o: Dr. Tamer started IV fluids in a young man whose blood pressure was not that low.
a.x: Ahmed should have been given water to drink instead.
a.w: He was confused, so drinking was unsafe, and heat stroke victims are often dry. IV fluids are part of standard care.

s:
Mrs. Sanaa, 72, came in weak and tired after a week of diarrhea from a stomach bug. She takes furosemide for her heart. Her ECG showed flat T waves and U waves, and her potassium came back at 2.4 mmol/L. Her kidneys were working normally.

Dr. Walid decided she needed potassium urgently. She could swallow, but felt sick. He put a cannula in a small vein on the back of her hand and wrote for 40 mmol of potassium chloride in 100 mL of saline to run over thirty minutes. He also asked for her magnesium to be checked and stopped her furosemide for now.

She had been drinking little because of nausea and had felt her heart skipping beats the night before. She lives alone, and her neighbor brought her in. Her other medicines are ramipril and aspirin. Her blood pressure was 112/70 and her pulse 88, with occasional extra beats. Her magnesium had not been checked yet.

He told her daughter the low potassium was from the diarrhea and the water tablet, and that she would need a few days in hospital. He asked for her to stay on a heart monitor while the potassium was being given.
h: 40 mmol of potassium chloride in 100 mL of saline to run over thirty minutes

a.o: Dr. Walid ran 40 mmol of potassium over thirty minutes through a small hand vein.
a.x: Potassium should have run at no more than 10 mmol an hour through a peripheral line.
a.w: Giving potassium too fast can stop the heart, and strong potassium burns small veins. Peripheral potassium is usually limited to about 10 mmol per hour.

a.o: Dr. Walid checked magnesium when the problem was potassium.
a.x: Magnesium was not relevant to her case.
a.w: Low magnesium is common with diarrhea and diuretics, and potassium won't stay up until magnesium is fixed.

a.o: Dr. Walid stopped her furosemide even though she has a heart condition.
a.x: She should have kept taking her furosemide.
a.w: Furosemide makes her lose more potassium. Pausing it while she is dry and low on potassium is sensible.

a.o: Dr. Walid put Mrs. Sanaa on a heart monitor for a simple salt problem.
a.x: The monitor was not needed.
a.w: Potassium of 2.4 with ECG changes can cause dangerous rhythms, so monitoring is right.

s:
Karim, 30, was stabbed once in the right side of his chest during a street fight. He was brought in sitting up, gasping and very pale. His breathing was fast at 36 a minute, his oxygen was 82 percent on a mask and his blood pressure 80/50.

Dr. Rana found no breath sounds on the right side, and the right side of his chest sounded hollow when tapped. The veins in his neck were swollen and his windpipe was pushed to the left.

The wound was a single 2 cm cut below the right nipple, no longer bleeding much. His friends said the knife had been a small kitchen knife. He was sweating, anxious and asking for water. The nurse had already cut his shirt off and covered the wound with a dressing taped on three sides.

She gave him high-flow oxygen, put in two large IV lines and asked for blood to be cross-matched. She called the porter to take him for an urgent chest X-ray to confirm a collapsed lung before putting in a chest drain. She asked the police officer who came with him to wait outside the resus room.
h: She called the porter to take him for an urgent chest X-ray to confirm a collapsed lung

a.o: Dr. Rana sent a man with a tension pneumothorax for an X-ray before releasing the pressure.
a.x: Karim should have had a needle or finger opening in his chest straight away, then a chest drain.
a.w: Low blood pressure, a shifted windpipe and an empty-sounding side mean tension pneumothorax. It is diagnosed by examination and treated at once; waiting for an X-ray can kill.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked the police officer to wait outside.
a.x: The officer should have stayed in the room since this was a crime.
a.w: Treatment comes first, and the patient's privacy matters. The police can talk to staff later.

a.o: Dr. Rana gave high-flow oxygen to a man who might have lung damage.
a.x: Oxygen should have been kept low.
a.w: Every badly injured patient gets high-flow oxygen at first.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked for blood to be cross-matched before knowing if he was bleeding.
a.x: Blood should be ordered only once bleeding is proven.
a.w: A stab wound with low blood pressure may be bleeding into the chest, so having blood ready is sensible.

t: Back pain that was an aneurysm
s:
Mr. Magdy, 71, a heavy smoker with high blood pressure, came in at midnight with sudden, severe pain in his lower back that spread to his belly. He had felt faint in the bathroom. His pulse was 110 and his blood pressure 96/60 in both arms.

Dr. Hossam found a tender, pulsing mass above his belly button. Mr. Magdy had a history of kidney stones, and his urine test showed a little blood.

His last kidney stone, two years ago, had felt "a bit like this, but not as bad". He had not passed urine since the pain started. His legs were pink with good pulses on both sides. He had eaten dinner at 8 p.m. and taken his amlodipine. His son said his father never complains of pain.

Dr. Hossam thought this was another kidney stone. He gave him IV morphine and diclofenac, put in a cannula and sent bloods including a cross-match. He booked a CT scan for the morning list and sent him to the observation ward. He asked the nurse to call him if the pain did not settle and documented that Mr. Magdy was "known stone former, likely renal colic".
h: He booked a CT scan for the morning list and sent him to the observation ward

a.o: Dr. Hossam treated a man with a pulsing belly mass and low blood pressure as a kidney stone and left him for a morning scan.
a.x: Mr. Magdy should have been seen urgently by the vascular surgeons for a likely ruptured aortic aneurysm.
a.w: An older smoker with sudden back pain, low blood pressure and a pulsing mass has a ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise. It needs surgery within hours.

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave morphine to a man with low blood pressure.
a.x: Pain relief should have waited until his pressure recovered.
a.w: Careful pain relief is fine even in a sick patient; untreated pain and fear also raise the pulse.

a.o: Dr. Hossam paid attention to a little blood in the urine, which proved a stone.
a.x: The urine result should have ended the search for other causes.
a.w: Blood in the urine is common in both stones and aneurysms, so it does not rule anything out.

a.o: Dr. Hossam sent a cross-match for a man he thought had a kidney stone.
a.x: Blood tests could have waited until the morning.
a.w: A man with low blood pressure needs blood ready; ordering it was the one sensible step.

s:
A family of four came in at 7 a.m. in winter: Mr. and Mrs. Gamal and their two children. All had woken up with headaches, nausea and dizziness. They live in a small flat and use a gas heater at night with the windows closed. The cat had been sleepy too.

Their oxygen saturations were all 98 to 100 percent on the finger probe. Mrs. Gamal, who is 14 weeks pregnant, felt the worst and was confused about the date. Their temperatures were normal.

The children, aged 6 and 9, were drowsy but answered questions. The headaches were worse in the morning and better on the way to hospital. Nobody had a fever or diarrhea. The family had eaten grilled chicken from a restaurant the night before. The flat's gas heater was new, installed by a neighbor last month.

Dr. Hany thought they had caught a stomach virus from a meal the night before. He gave them antiemetics and oral fluids, told them to rest and sent them home with advice to air the flat. He reassured them that their oxygen levels were perfect. He also wrote a sick note for Mr. Gamal and a school note for the children.
h: He reassured them that their oxygen levels were perfect

a.o: Dr. Hany trusted normal finger oxygen readings and sent home a whole family with headaches from a gas heater.
a.x: The family should have had carbon monoxide levels checked on a blood gas and been given high-flow oxygen.
a.w: A whole household with headache and nausea from a gas heater is carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. Finger probes read carboxyhemoglobin as normal oxygen, so they look falsely fine.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave sick and school notes to a family with a mild virus.
a.x: They should have been told to go to work and school.
a.w: Sick and school notes are reasonable for an acute illness and cost nothing.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked temperatures that had nothing to do with the problem.
a.x: Temperatures did not need checking.
a.w: A normal temperature helps argue against infection, so checking it was useful.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave antiemetics to a pregnant woman.
a.x: Mrs. Gamal should not have had any anti-sickness medicine.
a.w: Many antiemetics are safe in pregnancy; this was not the danger here.

s:
An old man known as Uncle Saber was found on a park bench at dawn after a cold, rainy night. He was wet, shivering only a little and mumbling. Passersby called an ambulance.

In the ER his core temperature was 31°C, his pulse 48 and his blood pressure 100/64. His ECG showed a slow rhythm with small extra notches on the QRS. His blood sugar was 4.8 mmol/L.

He had an empty bottle of cheap brandy in his coat. He was thin, with old scars on his hands, and staff at the shelter knew him well. He could not say his name clearly. His sugar was normal, and there were no obvious injuries. A nurse wrapped his head in a towel while warm blankets were fetched.

The team removed his wet clothes and covered him with warm blankets. Nurse Eman gave him warmed IV fluids. Dr. Ali asked her to put four hot water bottles on his arms and legs and to rub his limbs firmly to bring the blood back. He then booked him for a bed on the medical ward and asked social services to see him in the morning.
h: put four hot water bottles on his arms and legs and to rub his limbs firmly

a.o: Dr. Ali warmed Uncle Saber's arms and legs and had his limbs rubbed hard.
a.x: Uncle Saber should have been warmed from the core with warm blankets, warm air and fluids, and handled gently.
a.w: Rubbing and heating the limbs sends cold blood back to the heart and can cause a dangerous rhythm or a drop in pressure. Cold hearts are also easily upset by rough handling.

a.o: Nurse Eman gave warmed fluids through a drip to a man with a normal sugar.
a.x: Fluids should have waited until he had low sugar or low pressure.
a.w: Warmed IV fluids help rewarm from the inside and support blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ali booked Uncle Saber a medical ward bed instead of discharging him.
a.x: He should have gone home once he warmed up.
a.w: An older man with moderate hypothermia needs monitoring and a check for causes like infection or a stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ali asked social services to see Uncle Saber.
a.x: Social services should not have been involved.
a.w: A homeless older man with hypothermia needs help with shelter before he is discharged.

s:
Mr. Nabil, 47, came in at 3 a.m. with crushing central chest pain that started an hour earlier while he was sleeping. He was sweating and nauseous. His pulse was 92, blood pressure 140/86 and oxygen 97 percent.

His ECG showed ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Dr. Lamia gave him 300 mg of aspirin to chew and asked about bleeding problems; he had none. She called the cardiology team, who agreed to take him straight to the cath lab.

He was a smoker of 20 a day, had high cholesterol and took no regular medicines. His father had died of a heart attack at 60. He was frightened and asked if he was going to die. His wife had driven him in and was standing at the end of the trolley, holding his phone and wallet.

She gave him a small dose of IV morphine for the pain and an anti-sickness injection. She also put a second cannula in and asked his wife to sign the consent form for the procedure because he was in a lot of pain.
h: asked his wife to sign the consent form for the procedure because he was in a lot of pain

a.o: Dr. Lamia asked Mr. Nabil's wife to sign his consent form even though he was awake and able to decide.
a.x: Mr. Nabil should have been asked for consent himself, in simple words.
a.w: Pain alone does not take away a person's capacity. A conscious adult must consent for himself; his wife cannot sign for him.

a.o: Dr. Lamia gave aspirin before the cardiologists had seen him.
a.x: Aspirin should have waited for the cardiology team.
a.w: Aspirin is given as soon as a heart attack is suspected, if there is no bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Lamia put in a second cannula when one was enough.
a.x: One cannula was enough.
a.w: Two lines are useful in a heart attack in case of a sudden collapse.

a.o: Dr. Lamia sent Mr. Nabil to the cath lab instead of giving a clot-busting drug in the ER.
a.x: He should have had a clot-busting drug first.
a.w: When the cath lab can open the artery quickly, going straight there is better than clot-busting drugs.

t: Diabetic ketoacidosis with insulin before potassium
s:
Rawan, 17, has type 1 diabetes. She came in vomiting, breathing deeply and very thirsty after two days of a chest cold during which she skipped insulin because she was not eating.

Her blood sugar was 32 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, pH 7.08 and bicarbonate 8. Her pulse was 118 and blood pressure 104/66. Her potassium came back at 2.9 mmol/L.

Rawan was drowsy but answered questions. Her breath smelled fruity. She weighs 52 kg. Her chest X-ray showed a small patch of infection on the right. She had had DKA once before, two years ago. Her mother, who usually manages her insulin, had been away for three days for work.

Dr. Omar started a liter of saline over one hour and began an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour straight away. He planned to add potassium to the second bag of fluid. He asked for blood gases every hour and called her mother, who was at work, to come in. He also asked a nurse to measure her urine.
h: began an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour straight away

a.o: Dr. Omar started insulin while Rawan's potassium was only 2.9.
a.x: Rawan should have had potassium replaced first, and insulin started only once potassium was above 3.5.
a.w: Insulin drives potassium into the cells and can drop it to a level that stops the heart. A low potassium in DKA must be corrected before insulin.

a.o: Dr. Omar called Rawan's mother because she is under 18.
a.x: Rawan's mother should not have been told.
a.w: She is a minor and in a serious condition, so her parent should be informed and involved.

a.o: Dr. Omar ran saline quickly in a vomiting teenager.
a.x: Fluids should have been given slowly.
a.w: She was dry and in DKA; a liter over an hour is standard. Care is needed to avoid brain swelling but this pace was right.

a.o: Dr. Omar used a fixed insulin rate of 0.1 units/kg/hour instead of a sliding scale.
a.x: He should have used a sliding scale.
a.w: A fixed weight-based rate is the standard for DKA.

t: Shoulder put back without an X-ray
s:
Mostafa, 26, fell onto his outstretched arm while playing football. He came in holding his right arm away from his body and could not move his shoulder. The shoulder looked squared off and he had a lump in front of it.

Dr. Heba checked that he could feel the skin over the outside of his upper arm and that the pulse at his wrist was strong. She gave him IV morphine and laughing gas.

It was his third football injury this year, and he said his shoulder had "popped out" once before, three years ago, and gone back by itself. He was 70 kg, fit and healthy, and had eaten lunch two hours earlier. His friend, a physiotherapist, had already put his arm in a makeshift sling.

Because the dislocation was "obvious", she pulled his arm into place without an X-ray and felt a clunk. She then took an X-ray to make sure it was back in. The film showed the shoulder in place and a small crack in the upper arm bone she had not known about. She put him in a sling and booked him into the fracture clinic.
h: she pulled his arm into place without an X-ray

a.o: Dr. Heba put the shoulder back without an X-ray first, so she did not know a fracture was there.
a.x: Mostafa should have had an X-ray before the shoulder was moved.
a.w: A fracture near the shoulder can be pushed out of place during a reduction. A pre-reduction X-ray is the usual safe step.

a.o: Dr. Heba checked the feeling over Mostafa's upper arm before doing anything.
a.x: That check could have waited until after the shoulder was back.
a.w: Checking the axillary nerve before and after reduction is standard, to show whether any damage was there first.

a.o: Dr. Heba used laughing gas and morphine instead of a full anesthetic.
a.x: He should have had a general anesthetic.
a.w: Painkillers and gas are often enough for a shoulder reduction.

a.o: Dr. Heba sent Mostafa to the fracture clinic instead of the operating room.
a.x: He needed surgery straight away.
a.w: A small, stable crack can be followed up in the clinic.

s:
Mrs. Wafaa, 80, fell at home and hit her head. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. She came in drowsy, with vomiting and a headache. Her GCS was 13 and her blood pressure 150/90.

A CT scan showed a thin bleed over the surface of her brain. Her INR was 3.8. The neurosurgeons said they would watch her for now.

She lives with her son and uses a walking frame. Her blood pressure was steady and her pupils were equal. She had a small cut over her left eyebrow, which the nurse cleaned and closed with strips. Her platelets were normal. Her son said she had been on warfarin for six years without any problems.

Dr. Ziad stopped her warfarin and gave 1 mg of oral vitamin K. He planned to recheck her INR the next morning. He asked the nurses for neuro observations every hour and asked her son, who has power of attorney, about her wishes. He also wrote her a prescription for paracetamol for the headache and started IV fluids as she had been vomiting.
h: gave 1 mg of oral vitamin K. He planned to recheck her INR the next morning

a.o: Dr. Ziad tried to reverse Mrs. Wafaa's warfarin with a small oral dose of vitamin K for a brain bleed.
a.x: She should have had prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K straight away.
a.w: A bleed in the brain on warfarin needs fast, complete reversal. Oral vitamin K takes many hours to work.

a.o: Dr. Ziad stopped Mrs. Wafaa's warfarin even though she has atrial fibrillation.
a.x: Warfarin should have continued to protect her from a stroke.
a.w: With a bleed in the brain, the anticoagulant must stop; the risk of the bleed growing is much greater.

a.o: Dr. Ziad asked her son about her wishes instead of asking her.
a.x: He should have asked only Mrs. Wafaa.
a.w: She was drowsy, and her son holds a power of attorney, so it was reasonable to involve him.

a.o: Dr. Ziad gave paracetamol to an elderly woman with a head injury.
a.x: She should have had no painkillers.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe and doesn't increase bleeding.

s:
Mr. Hesham, 34, was found drowsy at home next to an empty box of amitriptyline. His wife said there had been 28 tablets of 50 mg. He was brought in two hours later.

He was drowsy, with a dry mouth, wide pupils and a pulse of 128. His blood pressure was 96/58. His ECG showed a QRS of 140 milliseconds. Shortly after, he had a brief seizure that stopped on its own.

His wife said he had been depressed since losing his business and had been prescribed the tablets three months ago. There was no alcohol involved as far as she knew. His temperature was 37.8°C and his bladder was full. He had no injuries from the seizure apart from a bitten tongue.

Dr. Mai protected his airway, gave oxygen and started IV fluids. She gave 4 mg of IV lorazepam for the seizure. Because he was getting drowsier, she put a breathing tube in to protect his airway and gave 50 g of activated charcoal through a stomach tube. She called the ICU and asked for his heart rhythm to be monitored. She did not give any other drugs because "the fluids should fix the pressure".
h: She did not give any other drugs because "the fluids should fix the pressure"

a.o: Dr. Mai did not give sodium bicarbonate to a man with a tricyclic overdose, a wide QRS and a seizure.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have had IV sodium bicarbonate right away.
a.w: A QRS over 100 ms in tricyclic overdose predicts seizures and deadly rhythms. Bicarbonate protects the heart and is the key treatment.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave lorazepam for a seizure that had already stopped.
a.x: She should have waited to see if another seizure came.
a.w: Benzodiazepines are reasonable after a seizure in a poisoned patient at risk of more.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave charcoal to a drowsy man who had just had a seizure.
a.x: Charcoal should not have been given at all.
a.w: Charcoal is risky in a drowsy patient only if the airway is unprotected. She put in a breathing tube first, and he came in within two hours.

a.o: Dr. Mai monitored his heart rhythm for a drug overdose.
a.x: Heart monitoring was not needed.
a.w: Tricyclics are dangerous to the heart, so monitoring is essential.

t: Sepsis missed in an older woman
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 84, came in from her care home because she was "not herself". She had been off her food for two days and had become muddled. The staff said she had been passing smelly urine.

At triage her temperature was 36.1°C, her pulse 112, breathing rate 24 and blood pressure 92/54. Her lactate was 3.6 mmol/L. Her urine dipstick showed nitrites and white cells.

She has dementia and lives in a care home, where she usually walks with a frame and chats to the staff. Today she was sleepy and pulling at her clothes. Her medicines include ramipril and a water tablet. Her lips were dry and her skin was cool. The carer who came with her had to leave after an hour.

Nurse Samar gave her a green card because her temperature was normal and she was "only confused". She noted the care home would be called and that a doctor would see her in about two hours. She gave her a cup of water and covered her with a blanket. She made sure her glasses and hearing aid were with her and that the care home had sent her medicines list.
h: gave her a green card because her temperature was normal

a.o: Nurse Samar triaged a confused older woman with a fast pulse, low pressure and high lactate as green because she had no fever.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have been treated as possible sepsis: urgent doctor review, blood cultures, IV antibiotics and fluids within the hour.
a.w: Older people often have no fever in sepsis. Confusion, low blood pressure, fast breathing and a high lactate are warning signs.

a.o: Nurse Samar gave her a cup of water.
a.x: She should have been kept nil by mouth.
a.w: A drink was fine; there was no plan for surgery.

a.o: Nurse Samar called the care home for information.
a.x: The care home should not have been contacted.
a.w: The care home knows her baseline and history, which helps.

a.o: Nurse Samar made sure Mrs. Nawal had her glasses and hearing aid.
a.x: These were not important.
a.w: Glasses and hearing aids help reduce confusion and fear.

s:
Malak, 8, was bitten on the hand by a neighbor's dog while playing in the street. Her mother brought her in about an hour later. The dog is vaccinated and the neighbor showed the certificate.

The bite left two deep puncture wounds and a 2 cm tear on the back of her hand. She could move all her fingers and feel everything. Her tetanus vaccines were up to date.

Malak was calm and had stopped crying by the time she was seen. The bites were on the back of her right hand over the knuckles. There was no sign of a broken bone on the X-ray. Her mother said the dog was usually friendly and Malak had pulled its tail. The neighbor promised to keep the dog home.

Dr. Khaled washed the wound well with plenty of saline. He then closed the tear and both punctures tightly with stitches so they would heal neatly. He gave a dose of paracetamol and sent her home without antibiotics because "the dog is vaccinated". He told her mother to come back if the hand became red or swollen.
h: He then closed the tear and both punctures tightly with stitches

a.o: Dr. Khaled stitched deep dog bite punctures shut and sent Malak home without antibiotics.
a.x: Malak's wounds should have been washed and left open, and she should have had a course of antibiotics.
a.w: Bites on the hand, especially deep punctures, have a high risk of infection. Closing them tightly traps bacteria inside.

a.o: Dr. Khaled did not give a tetanus shot.
a.x: She should have had a tetanus booster.
a.w: Her vaccines were up to date, so no booster was needed.

a.o: Dr. Khaled washed the wound with lots of saline instead of an antiseptic.
a.x: The wound should have been cleaned with strong antiseptic.
a.w: Plenty of saline washing is the best way to clean a bite.

a.o: Dr. Khaled did not give rabies vaccine.
a.x: Malak needed a rabies vaccine.
a.w: The dog was known, vaccinated and can be watched, so rabies treatment is not usually needed.

t: A burned airway left to swell
s:
Sami, 35, was burned when a gas cylinder exploded in his kitchen. He arrived an hour later. He weighs 80 kg. His face was red, his nose hairs were singed and his voice was getting hoarse. He had burns over the front of his chest and belly and the whole of both arms.

Dr. Nada estimated the burn at about 36 percent of his body. She covered the burns with cling film and gave IV morphine. She started fluids using the Parkland formula, worked out from the time of the burn, and put in a urinary catheter.

He had been trapped in the kitchen for a minute before neighbors pulled him out. He was coughing up black sputum. His oxygen was 95 percent on a mask. He had no other injuries and his blood pressure was normal. He was frightened and kept asking about his children, who were safe at school.

She noted his hoarse voice and singed nose hairs and wrote "airway: patent, talking, will reassess in an hour". She asked for a bed on the burns ward and gave him oxygen by mask. She called his wife to bring his medicines.
h: wrote "airway: patent, talking, will reassess in an hour"

a.o: Dr. Nada waited an hour to reassess Sami's airway even though he had singed nose hairs and a hoarse voice.
a.x: Sami should have been intubated early by an anesthetist before his airway swelled shut.
a.w: A hoarse voice and singed nose hairs after a fire in a closed space mean airway burns. Swelling can close the airway within hours and make intubation impossible.

a.o: Dr. Nada wrapped the burns in cling film.
a.x: The burns should have been covered with thick dressings.
a.w: Cling film is the recommended first cover for burns: clean, clear and painless.

a.o: Dr. Nada timed the fluids from the moment of the burn, not from arrival.
a.x: The fluid timing should have started when he arrived.
a.w: The Parkland formula is always counted from the time of the burn.

a.o: Dr. Nada put in a urinary catheter.
a.x: A catheter was not needed.
a.w: Urine output guides fluid replacement in big burns, so a catheter is essential.

s:
Doaa, 27, came in with pain on the lower left side of her belly and a little brown bleeding. Her last period was seven weeks ago. She had a coil removed last year and was trying for a baby.

Her pulse was 104 and blood pressure 108/70. Her belly was tender on the left, and she felt pain in the tip of her shoulder when she lay down. Her urine pregnancy test was positive.

She was pale and had fainted briefly in the bathroom at home that morning. She had had a chest infection last month and a sexually transmitted infection two years ago, which was treated. She had not eaten since breakfast and was very anxious about losing the baby. Her husband sat holding her hand.

Dr. Tarek thought she was having an early miscarriage. He did a quick bedside scan and saw an empty uterus. He told her the pregnancy had probably passed and sent her home with painkillers, asking her to repeat a pregnancy test in two weeks. He wrote the ward a note to say no scan was needed. He offered her a chaperone, which she accepted.
h: He told her the pregnancy had probably passed and sent her home with painkillers

a.o: Dr. Tarek sent home a pregnant woman with one-sided pain, shoulder tip pain and an empty uterus.
a.x: Doaa should have been treated as a possible ectopic pregnancy, with an urgent gynecology review and a formal scan.
a.w: An empty uterus with a positive test, one-sided pain and shoulder pain from blood under the diaphragm means a possible ruptured ectopic, which can kill.

a.o: Dr. Tarek did a scan at the bedside instead of sending her to radiology.
a.x: Only a formal radiology scan was acceptable.
a.w: A bedside scan is a quick, useful first look, though a formal scan was still needed.

a.o: Dr. Tarek offered a chaperone for her exam.
a.x: A chaperone was unnecessary.
a.w: A chaperone is good practice for intimate exams.

a.o: Dr. Tarek gave painkillers to a pregnant woman.
a.x: She should not have had any painkillers.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe in pregnancy.

s:
Habiba, 15, has asthma. She came in struggling to breathe after running a race. She could only say three or four words at a time. Her oxygen was 91 percent, her pulse 124 and her peak flow 40 percent of her best.

Nurse Iman gave her high-flow oxygen and nebulized salbutamol. Dr. Ehab added ipratropium to the nebulizer and gave her 40 mg of prednisolone by mouth. Habiba was very frightened and crying.

She had been coughing at night for a week and had not been using her brown preventer inhaler. She had been in intensive care for asthma once, at age 11. Her chest was tight, with a loud wheeze on both sides. She was sitting forward, gripping the edge of the trolley, her lips a little dusky.

To calm her down, Dr. Ehab gave her 2 mg of IV diazepam. He asked her mother to sit with her and wrote that she should be reassessed after the nebulizers. He planned to call the pediatric team if she did not improve.
h: To calm her down, Dr. Ehab gave her 2 mg of IV diazepam

a.o: Dr. Ehab gave a sedative to a teenager in the middle of a severe asthma attack.
a.x: Habiba should have been reassured and treated with more bronchodilators, never sedated.
a.w: Sedatives weaken the drive to breathe and can tip a severe asthma attack into respiratory failure.

a.o: Dr. Ehab gave steroids by mouth instead of by drip.
a.x: Steroids should have been given IV.
a.w: Oral prednisolone works as well as IV steroids if the patient can swallow.

a.o: Nurse Iman gave high-flow oxygen to a girl with asthma.
a.x: Oxygen should have been given at a low flow.
a.w: Asthma attacks need oxygen to keep saturations at 94 to 98 percent.

a.o: Dr. Ehab let Habiba's mother sit with her.
a.x: Her mother should have waited outside.
a.w: A parent calms a scared teenager, which helps her breathing.

t: Opioid overdose sent home too early
s:
Paramedics brought in Fady, 29, after friends found him blue and barely breathing at a party. They had given him 400 micrograms of naloxone into the muscle, and he woke up within two minutes. He admitted he had injected heroin and also taken some "long-acting" methadone tablets a friend gave him.

In the ER he was awake and chatty. His breathing rate was 14, oxygen 97 percent on air and his pupils normal-sized. He wanted to leave.

His friends said he had used heroin many times before but had never tried methadone. He had taken the tablets about an hour before he injected. He had no injuries, and his chest was clear. He had last eaten in the morning. He asked for a sandwich and some water, which the nurse brought.

Dr. Sara checked his sugar, which was normal, and cleaned a small abscess on his arm. She offered him a needle exchange leaflet and the number of an addiction service, which he took. Since he was now awake and breathing well, she agreed he could go home with his friends forty minutes after he arrived, without mentioning the methadone, and told him not to use alone. She documented that he had capacity to leave.
h: she agreed he could go home with his friends forty minutes after he arrived, without mentioning the methadone

a.o: Dr. Sara let Fady go home forty minutes after naloxone without warning him about the long-acting methadone.
a.x: Dr. Sara should have warned Fady clearly and urged him to stay for several hours of watching, with more naloxone ready.
a.w: Naloxone wears off within an hour, but methadone lasts much longer. He could stop breathing again at home.

a.o: Dr. Sara gave Fady a needle exchange leaflet instead of telling him to stop using.
a.x: She should have refused to support his drug use.
a.w: Harm reduction advice saves lives and does not encourage drug use.

a.o: Dr. Sara checked Fady's blood sugar after an opioid overdose.
a.x: A sugar check was pointless.
a.w: Low sugar can cause drowsiness too, so checking it in any drowsy patient is standard.

a.o: Dr. Sara wrote that Fady had capacity even though he uses drugs.
a.x: Drug users cannot be judged to have capacity.
a.w: Using drugs does not remove capacity; he was awake and could understand his choices. Capacity was not the real problem; the timing was.

s:
Mr. Samir, 59, was admitted at night with central chest pain that came on while climbing the stairs to his flat. The pain eased a little with rest but kept coming back. His ECG showed ST depression in the chest leads and his first troponin was raised.

On the morning round, Dr. Hala asked him about his medicines. He takes atorvastatin and ramipril, and he admitted, a little embarrassed, that he had taken sildenafil the evening before. His blood pressure was 134/82 and his pulse 76.

He had been a smoker until five years ago and has high blood pressure. His father died of a stroke. He said the pain was a tight band across his chest that went into his left arm. His oxygen was 97 percent on air, and his chest was clear. He was nervous about having an angiogram.

Dr. Hala started him on aspirin, a second antiplatelet and a blood thinner injection. When the pain came back during the round, she gave him a glyceryl trinitrate spray under the tongue and wrote for a nitrate infusion if it kept coming. She booked him for an angiogram the next day and explained the plan to his wife.
h: she gave him a glyceryl trinitrate spray under the tongue and wrote for a nitrate infusion

a.o: Dr. Hala gave nitrates to a man who had taken sildenafil less than a day before.
a.x: Mr. Samir should have had morphine or other pain relief and no nitrates for at least 24 hours after sildenafil.
a.w: Sildenafil and nitrates together can cause a sudden, deep drop in blood pressure that can be fatal.

a.o: Dr. Hala gave three blood-thinning drugs at once.
a.x: One antiplatelet drug was enough.
a.w: Aspirin, a second antiplatelet and an anticoagulant injection are standard for a heart attack with a raised troponin.

a.o: Dr. Hala booked an angiogram for the next day instead of that same hour.
a.x: He needed an angiogram immediately.
a.w: Without ST elevation, and with a stable pressure, an angiogram within 24 to 72 hours is usual unless pain or instability continues.

a.o: Dr. Hala discussed his sildenafil use in front of his wife.
a.x: The question should have been asked privately.
a.w: She asked him on his own during the round; the plan she later explained to his wife did not include private details.

s:
Mrs. Nadia, 38, came to the cardiology clinic for a routine check. Her blood pressure was 152/96 in the clinic and 148/94 when the nurse repeated it. She had brought her home readings for two weeks, all between 118/76 and 126/80, taken with a checked machine.

She is not a smoker, her cholesterol is normal and she exercises three times a week. Her ECG was normal and her urine test showed no protein.

She is a teacher and said she always felt nervous in clinics, especially after waiting an hour today. Her mother has high blood pressure and her father had a stroke at 70. Her BMI was 24. She drinks one coffee a day and does not drink alcohol. She takes no regular medicines and is not pregnant.

Dr. Fouad said her clinic readings were too high to ignore and started her on amlodipine 5 mg daily. He told her to stop measuring at home because "home machines are never accurate". He asked her to come back in three months for kidney tests and another reading. He also gave her a leaflet on cutting down salt.
h: started her on amlodipine 5 mg daily. He told her to stop measuring at home

a.o: Dr. Fouad started blood pressure pills based on clinic readings when Mrs. Nadia's careful home readings were all normal.
a.x: Dr. Fouad should have trusted her normal home readings as white coat hypertension and not started medicine.
a.w: High readings only in the clinic with normal home readings is white coat hypertension. Treatment is based on home or 24-hour readings.

a.o: Dr. Fouad did an ECG on a healthy young woman.
a.x: The ECG was not needed.
a.w: An ECG is part of the first check for anyone with raised blood pressure, to look for heart strain.

a.o: Dr. Fouad tested her urine for protein.
a.x: Urine was not relevant to blood pressure.
a.w: Protein in the urine is a sign of kidney damage from high blood pressure, so it is checked.

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave her a leaflet on salt.
a.x: She didn't need diet advice.
a.w: Cutting salt helps everyone's blood pressure; it does no harm.

s:
Mrs. Ola, 31, was admitted for three days with heart failure caused by a weak heart muscle after a viral infection. Her ejection fraction was 35 percent. She improved with IV furosemide.

On the day she went home, she mentioned she and her husband were hoping to have another baby soon. She was not pregnant now; her test was negative.

She has a two-year-old son and had breastfed for a year. She takes no other medicines and does not smoke. Her blood pressure on discharge was 108/68 and her pulse 72. Her kidney tests and potassium were normal. She asked whether the heart weakness could come back.

Dr. Mahmoud wrote her discharge plan: ramipril, bisoprolol and spironolactone, with furosemide as needed. He asked her to weigh herself every morning and come back if she gained 2 kg in three days. He booked a clinic visit in two weeks with kidney tests, and wrote that her heart drugs were "safe to continue if she gets pregnant". He gave her a heart failure booklet.
h: wrote that her heart drugs were "safe to continue if she gets pregnant"

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud told Mrs. Ola her ramipril and spironolactone were safe in pregnancy.
a.x: She should have been told these drugs harm a baby, advised to use contraception and to plan pregnancy with her cardiologist.
a.w: ACE inhibitors and spironolactone can damage an unborn baby. A woman planning pregnancy needs a clear warning and a plan.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud started her on a beta blocker while her heart was weak.
a.x: Beta blockers should be avoided in heart failure.
a.w: Beta blockers like bisoprolol, started once the patient is stable, help weak hearts live longer.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked her to weigh herself every day.
a.x: Weekly weighing was enough.
a.w: Daily weights catch fluid building up early.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud booked kidney tests in two weeks.
a.x: The kidney tests could wait for six months.
a.w: Ramipril and spironolactone can raise potassium and affect the kidneys, so early checks are needed.

s:
Mr. Hassan, 73, has a mechanical mitral valve and takes warfarin. His INR has been stable between 2.5 and 3.5 for a year. He was admitted with a chest infection and was confused for a day.

Dr. Nihal started IV ceftriaxone, then switched him to clarithromycin by mouth because his chest X-ray suggested an atypical infection. She continued his usual warfarin dose and booked his next INR for the following week at his clinic, as usual.

He lives with his wife and keeps a small book of his INR results, which he showed Dr. Nihal proudly. His kidneys were normal. He coughed up green sputum and had a fever of 38.4°C on admission. He had no bleeding, and his valve clicked crisply when she listened.

She also stopped his evening glass of grapefruit juice, which she had read could interfere with medicines. She asked the physiotherapist to help him walk and made sure he had his hearing aids in.
h: booked his next INR for the following week at his clinic, as usual

a.o: Dr. Nihal started clarithromycin with warfarin but left the next INR check for a week.
a.x: Mr. Hassan's INR should have been checked within a few days, and his dose adjusted.
a.w: Clarithromycin strongly raises warfarin levels. With a mechanical valve and an infection, his INR could rise fast and cause a bleed.

a.o: Dr. Nihal stopped his grapefruit juice.
a.x: The juice was harmless and should have stayed.
a.w: Grapefruit affects some drugs; stopping it during illness does no harm.

a.o: Dr. Nihal switched from IV to oral antibiotics while he was still unwell.
a.x: IV antibiotics should have continued.
a.w: Switching to oral once a patient is improving is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Nihal kept the same warfarin dose.
a.x: She should have halved his warfarin dose.
a.w: With a mechanical valve, stopping or halving warfarin risks a clot. Monitoring was the gap, not the dose.

s:
Mr. Atef, 66, has had a heart attack and takes atorvastatin 80 mg. He came to clinic with three weeks of aching thighs and dark brown urine. He had started a course of an antibiotic from his GP for a chest infection a few days before the aches began.

Dr. Karim found his thighs tender. His kidney tests were normal last month.

He also takes aspirin, bisoprolol and ramipril. He had felt more tired than usual and could hardly climb the stairs to his flat. The antibiotic from the GP was clarithromycin, which he had finished two days ago. His wife said he had been drinking less water because of the heat.

Dr. Karim told him statin aches are common and nothing to worry about. He asked him to keep taking the statin because "stopping after a heart attack is too dangerous", gave him paracetamol and booked a routine follow-up in three months. He praised Mr. Atef for walking every day and told him to keep it up.
h: He asked him to keep taking the statin

a.o: Dr. Karim told Mr. Atef to keep taking his statin despite tender thighs and dark urine.
a.x: Dr. Karim should have stopped the statin and checked his CK and kidneys urgently.
a.w: Muscle pain with dark urine suggests muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis). It can damage the kidneys and is a reason to stop the statin.

a.o: Dr. Karim prescribed paracetamol for the aches.
a.x: He should have prescribed ibuprofen.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe for muscle aches; ibuprofen could stress the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Karim encouraged Mr. Atef to keep walking daily.
a.x: He should have told him to rest.
a.w: Exercise is good for heart patients; his aches were not caused by walking.

a.o: Dr. Karim used a high statin dose in an older man.
a.x: A low dose was enough after a heart attack.
a.w: High-intensity statins are standard after a heart attack.

t: Two beta blockers, one from the eyes
s:
Mrs. Samah, 76, felt dizzy and fainted twice this week. She takes bisoprolol 10 mg for atrial fibrillation and has started eye drops for glaucoma two weeks ago. Her pulse was 38 and her blood pressure 98/56.

Her ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a slow rate. Her potassium and thyroid tests were normal.

She lives with her daughter and walks with a stick. She had felt light-headed for two weeks, worse when standing. Her blood pressure dropped to 86/50 when she stood. She had no chest pain. Her ECG showed no signs of a heart attack, and her troponin was normal.

Dr. Hossam stopped her bisoprolol and asked about her eye drops, which were timolol, also a beta blocker. He told her to stop those too and called her eye doctor to switch them. He put her on a heart monitor and kept her in hospital. He explained that a pacemaker might be needed if her pulse stayed slow. He asked her daughter, who lives with her, to help her get up slowly.
h: He told her to stop those too and called her eye doctor to switch them

a.o: Mrs. Samah's eye doctor had started timolol eye drops on top of her bisoprolol without checking her heart drugs.
a.x: Her eye doctor should have chosen a glaucoma drop that is not a beta blocker.
a.w: Timolol drops get into the blood and add to bisoprolol, slowing the heart dangerously. The flaw happened before admission.

a.o: Dr. Hossam stopped her bisoprolol even though she has atrial fibrillation.
a.x: Bisoprolol should have continued.
a.w: A pulse of 38 with fainting means the dose is too strong; stopping it is right.

a.o: Dr. Hossam talked about a pacemaker too early.
a.x: He should not have mentioned a pacemaker.
a.w: It is fair to warn a patient about a possible next step.

a.o: Dr. Hossam kept her in hospital for a slow pulse.
a.x: She could have gone home.
a.w: Fainting with a pulse of 38 needs monitoring.

s:
Mr. Rafik, 81, has heart failure and atrial fibrillation. He takes digoxin, furosemide 80 mg twice a day and apixaban. He came in with nausea, loss of appetite and seeing yellow haloes around lights.

His pulse was 52 and irregular. His potassium was 2.9 mmol/L and his creatinine had risen from 110 to 180. His digoxin level was high. His ECG showed some extra beats.

He lives alone and his daughter fills his weekly pill box. She said he had been taking extra furosemide because his ankles were puffy. He had vomited twice and had eaten very little for four days. His blood pressure was 104/64 and his chest was clear apart from a few crackles at the bases.

Dr. Yasmin held his digoxin. She increased his furosemide to 120 mg twice a day to "dry him out" because his ankles were a little puffy. She lowered his apixaban to 2.5 mg twice a day because of his age and kidneys and asked for daily kidney tests. She asked the dietitian to see him because he was eating little.
h: She increased his furosemide to 120 mg twice a day

a.o: Dr. Yasmin increased Mr. Rafik's water pills while his potassium was low, his kidneys were worse and he had digoxin poisoning.
a.x: His furosemide should have been reduced, potassium replaced, and digoxin antibody considered if his rhythm worsened.
a.w: More diuretic lowers potassium further and harms the kidneys, which makes digoxin toxicity worse.

a.o: Dr. Yasmin held his digoxin.
a.x: Digoxin should have continued for his atrial fibrillation.
a.w: Digoxin toxicity means the drug must stop.

a.o: Dr. Yasmin kept a blood thinner going while his kidneys were getting worse.
a.x: His apixaban should have been stopped completely.
a.w: Apixaban can continue at a lower dose for his age and kidneys. Stopping it would leave him open to a stroke from his atrial fibrillation.

a.o: Dr. Yasmin asked the dietitian to see an elderly man.
a.x: Diet was not important.
a.w: Poor eating in heart failure is common and needs support.

s:
Ziad, 17, plays midfield for a football academy. He fainted during a training sprint last week. His uncle died suddenly at 34. On listening, Dr. Sherine heard a murmur that got louder when he stood up from squatting.

His ECG showed very tall voltages and deep T wave inversion. An echo showed a thick heart wall of 24 mm with blockage of the outflow tract.

He had felt his heart race a few times during training this season but kept quiet so he would not lose his place in the team. He doesn't smoke, drink or take supplements. His blood pressure was 118/70. His mother had come with him and was very anxious about what would happen to his football career.

Dr. Sherine started bisoprolol and arranged a heart monitor and a heart MRI. She referred him for an ICD assessment and genetic testing and suggested screening his parents and siblings. She told him he could keep training lightly but could still play matches "as long as he takes his tablets". She wrote a note for his coach.
h: could still play matches "as long as he takes his tablets"

a.o: Dr. Sherine allowed Ziad to keep playing competitive matches with a thick heart wall, fainting and a family history of sudden death.
a.x: Ziad should have been told to stop competitive sport until the full assessment, and an ICD considered.
a.w: Fainting on exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a high-risk sign. Intense sport can trigger fatal rhythms.

a.o: Dr. Sherine suggested screening his family.
a.x: His family did not need tests.
a.w: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is often inherited, so first-degree relatives should be screened.

a.o: Dr. Sherine started a beta blocker.
a.x: A beta blocker was not needed.
a.w: Beta blockers ease outflow blockage and symptoms.

a.o: Dr. Sherine arranged an MRI after an echo already showed the problem.
a.x: The echo was enough.
a.w: MRI shows scarring that helps predict sudden death risk.

t: Pericarditis treated as a heart attack
s:
Yara, 28, came in with sharp chest pain that was worse when she breathed in and lay flat, and better when she leaned forward. She had a cold a week ago. Her temperature was 37.9°C.

Dr. Ahmed heard a scratchy sound over her heart. Her ECG showed ST elevation in almost every lead with PR depression. Her troponin was normal and her echo showed a small amount of fluid around the heart with normal pumping.

She is a nurse who works night shifts and takes no medicines apart from the pill. She doesn't smoke. Her blood pressure was 116/74 and pulse 104. Her chest X-ray was normal. She was worried because a colleague had a heart attack at a young age last year.

Dr. Ahmed called the cath lab for an emergency angiogram as a heart attack. He gave her aspirin, ticagrelor and heparin. He also asked for her pregnancy test, which was negative. He asked her partner to bring her overnight bag.
h: Dr. Ahmed called the cath lab for an emergency angiogram as a heart attack

a.o: Dr. Ahmed treated Yara's pericarditis as a heart attack and sent her for an angiogram on blood thinners.
a.x: Yara should have been treated for pericarditis with NSAIDs and colchicine, and her blood thinners avoided.
a.w: Widespread ST elevation with PR depression, pain eased by leaning forward and a rub after a cold is pericarditis. Heparin can cause bleeding into the sac around the heart.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed checked for pregnancy.
a.x: A pregnancy test was not needed.
a.w: Any young woman getting X-rays or drugs should have pregnancy ruled out.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed did an echo.
a.x: An echo was not needed.
a.w: An echo checks for fluid around the heart, which is important in pericarditis.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed asked her partner to bring her bag.
a.x: She should have gone home that night.
a.w: Staying for observation was fine.

s:
Mr. Nour, 45, has a mechanical aortic valve and takes warfarin. He came to clinic asking about a dental visit next week for a deep cleaning and a filling. His INR was 2.8.

Dr. Lobna examined his mouth and saw inflamed gums. His valve sounded crisp and his echo last year was normal.

He had the valve replaced four years ago for rheumatic heart disease. He takes his warfarin in the evening and checks his INR every two weeks. His dentist had asked him to get a letter from his cardiologist before the visit. He said his gums bled sometimes when he brushed.

She told him he could go ahead, keep his warfarin at the same dose and asked the dentist to use local measures to stop bleeding. She told him he did not need antibiotics before the cleaning because "that is old advice". She also reminded him to brush twice a day and see his dentist every six months.
h: She told him he did not need antibiotics before the cleaning because "that is old advice"

a.o: Dr. Lobna told a man with a mechanical heart valve that he did not need antibiotics before a deep dental cleaning.
a.x: Mr. Nour should have had antibiotics before the dental work.
a.w: A mechanical valve is a high-risk heart condition. Antibiotics are still advised for dental work that disturbs the gums.

a.o: Dr. Lobna let him keep taking warfarin for the dental work.
a.x: His warfarin should have been stopped for three days.
a.w: Stopping warfarin with a mechanical valve risks clots; dentists can control minor bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Lobna told him to brush twice a day.
a.x: This advice was unnecessary.
a.w: Good dental care lowers the risk of infection on his valve.

a.o: Dr. Lobna checked his mouth at a heart clinic.
a.x: That was the dentist's job.
a.w: Gum disease raises the risk of valve infection, so it's relevant.

s:
Mrs. Rasha, 72, was admitted with a chest infection. Her ECG showed atrial fibrillation, which was new. She has high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. She had no history of bleeding and her kidneys were normal.

Her pulse came down from 130 to 88 after bisoprolol. She felt well enough to go home after five days of antibiotics.

She lives with her husband and is independent. She had never had a stroke or mini-stroke. She takes metformin and amlodipine. She told Dr. Fady she was scared of blood thinners because her sister had a nosebleed on one. Her blood pressure on discharge was 136/80.

Dr. Fady discussed her rhythm with her. He worked out her CHA2DS2-VASc score as 4 but said that since her rhythm might go back to normal after the infection, she would only need aspirin for now. He booked a heart rhythm check in three months. He also made sure she had a flu vaccine before she left.
h: she would only need aspirin for now

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Rasha aspirin instead of an anticoagulant despite a high stroke risk score.
a.x: She should have started an anticoagulant like apixaban.
a.w: A CHA2DS2-VASc of 4 means a high stroke risk. Aspirin does not prevent strokes in atrial fibrillation well.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave bisoprolol to slow her heart.
a.x: She needed her rhythm shocked back to normal.
a.w: Rate control with a beta blocker is a standard first step.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave a flu vaccine in hospital.
a.x: Vaccines should wait until full recovery.
a.w: Vaccinating a recovering older patient is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Fady booked a rhythm check in three months.
a.x: It should be checked the next day.
a.w: A follow-up check is reasonable.

t: Aortic stenosis and a fall in pressure
s:
Mr. Ehab, 84, has severe aortic stenosis and is waiting for a valve replacement. He was admitted with a chest infection and some breathlessness. His blood pressure was 112/70.

Dr. Abeer heard a soft second heart sound and a harsh murmur reaching his neck. His echo last month showed a valve area of 0.7 cm².

He had become more breathless over the past month and had fainted once while gardening. He lives with his son. His kidney function was mildly reduced. His oxygen was 93 percent on air. His chest X-ray showed a patch of infection on the left and a large heart.

His GP had recently added ramipril. Dr. Abeer started IV antibiotics and, because his ankles were swollen, gave him a nitrate infusion to "take the load off his heart". She asked the physio to see him and talked to his son about the valve surgery plan.
h: gave him a nitrate infusion to "take the load off his heart"

a.o: Dr. Abeer started a nitrate infusion in a man with severe aortic stenosis.
a.x: Mr. Ehab's swollen ankles should have been treated with careful diuretics, and nitrates avoided.
a.w: A tight aortic valve means the heart can't increase its output. Nitrates widen the vessels and can drop the pressure dangerously.

a.o: Dr. Abeer started IV antibiotics.
a.x: Oral antibiotics were enough.
a.w: IV antibiotics are reasonable in an older man with an infection and breathlessness.

a.o: Dr. Abeer discussed surgery with his son.
a.x: The surgery plan should be discussed only with Mr. Ehab.
a.w: Including family with the patient's agreement is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked a physiotherapist to see him.
a.x: Physio was unnecessary.
a.w: Physio helps an older patient recover from a chest infection.

s:
Mr. Kamal, 62, came to clinic six weeks after a heart attack and a stent in his front artery. He said he felt well and was walking 30 minutes a day.

His blood pressure was 128/78 and his LDL cholesterol 1.6 mmol/L. His echo showed a pumping function of 55 percent.

He had gone back to his job as an accountant part-time and had stopped smoking after the heart attack. He was eating less fried food and had lost 3 kg. He asked whether he could start swimming again. He had no chest pain and no bruising or bleeding.

He had stopped his clopidogrel two weeks earlier because a neighbor said it made people bleed. Dr. Ihab praised his walking and his cholesterol. He told him to keep his aspirin and statin, booked an exercise test and wrote him a sick note for another two weeks. He did not mention the clopidogrel because "aspirin alone is enough now".
h: He did not mention the clopidogrel because "aspirin alone is enough now"

a.o: Dr. Ihab accepted that Mr. Kamal stopped clopidogrel six weeks after a stent.
a.x: Mr. Kamal should have restarted clopidogrel and been told why both drugs are needed for a year.
a.w: Stopping one of the two antiplatelets early after a stent can cause a clot in the stent and another heart attack.

a.o: Dr. Ihab praised Mr. Kamal for walking 30 minutes a day.
a.x: He should have been told to rest.
a.w: Walking is good for heart recovery.

a.o: Dr. Ihab booked an exercise test.
a.x: The test was unnecessary.
a.w: An exercise test helps plan safe activity.

a.o: Dr. Ihab wrote a sick note for two more weeks.
a.x: He should have gone back to work at once.
a.w: A short extra rest is reasonable.

s:
Mrs. Hanan, 69, was brought in at night, sitting bolt upright and gasping. She has a weak heart from an old heart attack. Her oxygen was 84 percent, her pulse 118 and her blood pressure 172/98. She had crackles up to the middle of both lungs and swollen legs.

Dr. Bassem gave her oxygen and sat her up. Her chest X-ray showed fluid in the lungs.

She had run out of her furosemide five days ago and had eaten a salty family meal at a wedding the night before. She takes bisoprolol and ramipril. Her kidney function was mildly reduced, as it had been at her last clinic visit. She was frightened and kept trying to pull off the oxygen mask.

Because she had not passed much urine that day, he thought she might be dry. He ran 500 mL of saline over thirty minutes and asked the nurse to check her urine output. He also gave her a nitrate spray and put her on CPAP when her oxygen did not improve. He asked the ward to keep a bed for her.
h: He ran 500 mL of saline over thirty minutes

a.o: Dr. Bassem gave a fluid bolus to a woman drowning in fluid from heart failure.
a.x: Mrs. Hanan should have had IV furosemide, not fluids.
a.w: Crackles, swollen legs, high pressure and fluid on the X-ray show fluid overload. Extra fluid makes it worse.

a.o: Dr. Bassem gave a nitrate spray.
a.x: Nitrates should be avoided.
a.w: With a high blood pressure, nitrates reduce the load on the heart.

a.o: Dr. Bassem put her on CPAP.
a.x: CPAP was too much.
a.w: CPAP helps push fluid out of the lungs when oxygen alone fails.

a.o: Dr. Bassem sat her upright.
a.x: She should have lain flat.
a.w: Sitting up eases breathing in heart failure.

t: Long QT and a new antibiotic
s:
