Mrs. Nawal, 61, has had short spinning attacks for two weeks, each lasting less than a minute. They happen when she turns over in bed or looks up to hang the washing. She has no hearing loss, ringing, headache or weakness.

Dr. Ihab did a test where he turned her head to the right and laid her back quickly. Her eyes flickered in a twisting pattern for twenty seconds and she felt dizzy. Her neurological exam was normal.

He explained that this was benign positional vertigo, caused by small crystals in the inner ear. He told her it was not dangerous and that it often settles.

He prescribed betahistine and prochlorperazine to take every day for three months. He did not try any head movements to treat it, saying "the tablets will settle it".
h: He prescribed betahistine and prochlorperazine to take every day for three months

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave long-term tablets for positional vertigo and did not treat it with a head maneuver.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had the Epley maneuver in clinic, which moves the crystals back.
a.w: BPPV is treated with the Epley maneuver. Long-term sedating tablets slow recovery and raise the risk of falls in older people.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told her it was not dangerous.
a.x: He should have warned her it might be a stroke.
a.w: Short positional spinning with a normal exam and a positive test is BPPV, which is harmless.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a test that made her dizzy.
a.x: The test was cruel.
a.w: The Dix-Hallpike test confirms BPPV.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her nervous system.
a.x: That was unnecessary.
a.w: A normal neurological exam helps rule out a stroke.

s:
Fares, 3, was brought in by his mother because he had pushed a bead up his right nostril an hour ago. He was breathing fine and playing. There was no bleeding. Mrs. Laila had tried to pull it out with tweezers at home but could not reach it.

Dr. Omar looked in Fares's nose with a light and saw a round, shiny bead just inside the right nostril. Fares was calm on his mother's lap.

Dr. Omar explained to the mother that he would try to get the bead out. He asked her to cover her mouth over Fares's mouth and blow gently while blocking the other nostril, "the mother's kiss". When this didn't work, he tried to grab the bead with long tweezers.

The smooth bead slipped back further. Dr. Omar kept trying with the tweezers four more times while Fares cried and struggled. He wrote "foreign body in situ, try again tomorrow".
h: Dr. Omar kept trying with the tweezers four more times while Fares cried and struggled

a.o: Dr. Omar kept trying to grab a smooth bead with tweezers, pushing it further back while the child struggled.
a.x: After the first failed attempt, Fares should have been referred to ENT for removal with the right tools.
a.w: Round objects slip from tweezers and can be pushed back into the airway. Repeated tries on a struggling child are unsafe.

a.o: Dr. Omar tried the "mother's kiss".
a.x: That was unsafe.
a.w: The mother's kiss is a safe first try for nasal foreign bodies.

a.o: Dr. Omar looked with a light.
a.x: A scan was needed.
a.w: Looking with a light is enough to see a bead near the nostril.

a.o: Dr. Omar let Fares sit on his mother's lap.
a.x: Fares should have been held flat.
a.w: A calm child on a parent's lap is easier to examine.

s:
Hana, 22, had her tonsils removed eight days ago. She came in after spitting out a small amount of fresh blood twice in the evening. She had been eating normally and taking ibuprofen and paracetamol for the pain.

Dr. Mohamed found a small clot on the left tonsil bed. Her pulse was 96 and her blood pressure normal. Her blood count was normal. The bleeding had stopped.

He told her that some bleeding is common around day seven to ten after the operation, as the scabs come off. He asked her to gargle with cold water.

As she looked well and the bleeding had stopped, he sent her home and told her to come back if it bled again. He did not call ENT or keep her for observation.
h: he sent her home and told her to come back if it bled again

a.o: Dr. Mohamed sent home a woman who had bled from her tonsil bed instead of keeping her for observation.
a.x: Hana should have been admitted under ENT for observation and treatment, even though it had stopped.
a.w: A small bleed after tonsillectomy can come before a big one. Patients are kept in hospital to watch.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed said bleeding is common at day seven to ten.
a.x: Bleeding after a week is never normal.
a.w: Secondary bleeding is most common between days five and ten.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed checked her blood count.
a.x: The blood count was unnecessary.
a.w: A blood count helps judge how much she had lost.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed told her to gargle cold water.
a.x: Gargling was dangerous.
a.w: Cold water can help small vessels close.

t: Hearing aid for a blocked ear
s:
Mr. Fouad, 74, came to clinic with his wife, who said he turned the television up too loud and kept asking her to repeat herself. He felt he could hear well in quiet rooms but not in busy places. He has worked in a factory for forty years.

Dr. Hala looked in both ears and found both canals completely blocked with hard wax. She could not see either eardrum.

She explained that hearing often gets worse with age and noise. She asked about dizziness and ringing, which he did not have.

She sent him for a hearing test and fitting of hearing aids, writing "age-related hearing loss". She did not treat the wax first.
h: She sent him for a hearing test and fitting of hearing aids, writing "age-related hearing loss". She did not treat the wax first

a.o: Dr. Hala sent Mr. Fouad for hearing aids without clearing the wax that blocked both ears.
a.x: The wax should have been removed first, with a hearing test afterwards.
a.w: Wax blocking the canals can cause a big hearing loss. Hearing tests and aid fittings are not accurate until it is cleared.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked about dizziness and ringing.
a.x: That was not relevant.
a.w: Dizziness or ringing may point to other ear problems.

a.o: Dr. Hala said hearing often gets worse with age and noise.
a.x: She should have said nothing.
a.w: Age and noise are common causes of hearing loss.

a.o: Dr. Hala talked to his wife.
a.x: She should have spoken only to Mr. Fouad.
a.w: His wife gave useful information about his hearing at home, with him present.

s:
Mrs. Basma, 44, woke up yesterday with the right side of her face drooping. She could not close her right eye properly, her mouth drooped and her food collected in her right cheek. Sounds were loud in her right ear. She had pain behind the ear the day before.

Dr. Mahmoud found weakness of the whole right face, including the forehead. Her ears looked normal with no blisters. Her arms and legs were normal. Her blood sugar and blood pressure were normal.

He explained that this was Bell's palsy, a nerve problem that usually gets better on its own. He prescribed prednisolone for ten days, starting today.

He told her it would probably recover in a few weeks to months. He did not give any eye drops or advice about her eye, which kept watering, "since it will recover".
h: He did not give any eye drops or advice about her eye

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud did not protect Mrs. Basma's eye, which could not close.
a.x: She should have been given lubricating eye drops by day, ointment at night and told to tape the eye shut while sleeping.
a.w: An eye that can't close dries out and can be scratched, leading to ulcers and loss of sight.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud gave steroids within 72 hours.
a.x: Steroids don't help Bell's palsy.
a.w: Steroids started within 72 hours improve recovery.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her ears for blisters.
a.x: Ears are not linked to the face.
a.w: Blisters in the ear would suggest shingles of the facial nerve, which needs antivirals.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her arms and legs.
a.x: That was unnecessary.
a.w: A normal limb exam helps rule out a stroke.

t: Child with glue ear and speech delay
s:
Mostafa, 4, came in with his parents because his nursery said his speech was behind. He often said "what?" and sat close to the TV. He had several ear infections last winter. He snores at night.

Dr. Ayman found dull, retracted eardrums on both sides with a fluid level. A hearing test showed a moderate loss in both ears. His tonsils were large.

He explained that this was glue ear, fluid behind the eardrums, common after colds. He said it often clears on its own and suggested waiting three months.

He then repeated the hearing test after three months, which still showed a moderate loss. He told them it would clear by itself eventually and booked another check in a year, with no other plan.
h: booked another check in a year, with no other plan

a.o: Dr. Ayman left glue ear with lasting hearing loss and speech delay for another year.
a.x: Mostafa should have been offered grommets or hearing aids after the three-month wait.
a.w: Glue ear that lasts three months with hearing loss and speech delay needs treatment, because hearing affects speech and learning.

a.o: Dr. Ayman suggested waiting three months first.
a.x: He should have operated at once.
a.w: Most glue ear clears within three months.

a.o: Dr. Ayman did a hearing test.
a.x: A hearing test was not needed.
a.w: A hearing test shows how much the fluid affects hearing.

a.o: Dr. Ayman explained glue ear is common.
a.x: He should have said it is rare.
a.w: Glue ear is very common in young children.

t: Sinusitis given antibiotics at day two
s:
Mrs. Inas, 36, came in with a blocked nose, a pressure feeling over her cheeks and a clear runny nose for two days. She had a slight temperature and a sore throat. She was otherwise healthy. She was worried because she was travelling for work next week.

Dr. Hossam found mild tenderness over her cheeks and a red nasal lining. Her temperature was 37.6°C. Her throat was a little red and her chest clear.

He explained that most sinus infections are caused by viruses and clear up in ten days. He advised saline nose rinses, a steroid nasal spray and painkillers.

Because she was travelling, he also prescribed co-amoxiclav for a week. He told her to come back if she was not better in ten days.
h: Because she was travelling, he also prescribed co-amoxiclav for a week

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave antibiotics for two days of sinus symptoms.
a.x: Mrs. Inas should have been managed without antibiotics unless symptoms lasted over ten days or got much worse.
a.w: Early sinusitis is almost always viral. Antibiotics don't help and cause side effects.

a.o: Dr. Hossam advised a steroid nasal spray.
a.x: Steroids are dangerous in infection.
a.w: Steroid nasal sprays ease swelling in sinusitis.

a.o: Dr. Hossam advised saline rinses.
a.x: Rinses don't help.
a.w: Saline rinses clear mucus and ease symptoms.

a.o: Dr. Hossam said most sinus infections clear in ten days.
a.x: They usually last a month.
a.w: Viral sinusitis usually improves within ten days.

s:
Mohamed, 19, was punched in the face during a football match. His nose bled for ten minutes and then stopped. He came in two hours later. His nose was swollen and bent to the left. He was breathing through both sides.

Dr. Eman checked inside his nose with a light and saw a purple swelling on the middle wall that blocked the left nostril. It was soft when she pressed it. He had no clear fluid from his nose and no double vision.

She explained that the nose was probably broken and that the swelling would settle. She told him to put ice on it and take paracetamol. She booked an ENT clinic visit in a week to check whether it needed straightening.

She did not mention the swelling on the middle wall of the nose and wrote "nasal fracture, ENT clinic 1 week".
h: She did not mention the swelling on the middle wall of the nose

a.o: Dr. Eman did not arrange urgent drainage of a blood collection on the nasal septum.
a.x: Mohamed should have been seen by ENT the same day to drain the septal hematoma.
a.w: A septal hematoma can cut off blood to the cartilage, leading to an abscess and a collapsed nose within days.

a.o: Dr. Eman booked ENT clinic in a week for the broken nose.
a.x: The nose should have been straightened that day.
a.w: Swelling must settle before a broken nose is judged; five to ten days is usual.

a.o: Dr. Eman checked for clear fluid from his nose.
a.x: That was not needed.
a.w: Clear fluid could mean a skull base fracture.

a.o: Dr. Eman advised ice.
a.x: Heat is better.
a.w: Ice reduces swelling.

t: One-sided nasal blockage in an adult
s:
Mr. Hesham, 56, a carpenter, came in with a blocked left nostril for four months. He sometimes had blood-stained mucus from that side and a reduced sense of smell. He had lost some weight. He has worked with hardwood dust for thirty years.

Dr. Nesma looked inside with a light and saw a red, swollen area high in the left nostril. The right side was clear. He had no neck lumps. His eye movements were normal.

She explained that this was probably a polyp from allergy and gave him a steroid nasal spray for three months. She told him to rinse with salt water.

She booked him back in three months, and wrote "nasal polyps, trial of steroids". She did not arrange a scope or a scan.
h: She did not arrange a scope or a scan

a.o: Dr. Nesma treated one-sided nasal blockage with bleeding in a woodworker as polyps without a scope or scan.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have been urgently referred for a nasal endoscopy and scan to rule out a tumor.
a.w: Polyps are usually on both sides. One-sided blockage with bleeding, weight loss and wood dust exposure can be a nose or sinus cancer.

a.o: Dr. Nesma asked about his work.
a.x: His job was irrelevant.
a.w: Hardwood dust is linked to nasal cancer.

a.o: Dr. Nesma checked his eye movements.
a.x: The eyes are not part of a nose exam.
a.w: Eye problems can mean a growth spreading from the sinuses.

a.o: Dr. Nesma checked for neck lumps.
a.x: Neck lumps were not relevant.
a.w: Neck lumps can be a sign of cancer spreading.

s:
Mrs. Ola, 49, came in two hours after eating fish for lunch. She felt something sharp stuck in her throat on the right side, just above her collarbone. Swallowing hurt and she could swallow her saliva only slowly. She had no breathing difficulty.

Dr. Ahmed looked in her mouth and at her tonsils with a light and saw no bone. Her neck was not swollen. Her voice was normal.

He explained that sometimes a bone scratches the throat and leaves a feeling that it is still there. He told her to eat soft bread to push it down.

He sent her home with painkillers and told her to come back if she was not better in a week. He did not arrange a scope or X-ray.
h: He did not arrange a scope or X-ray

a.o: Dr. Ahmed sent home a woman with a fish bone feeling low in her throat, pain on swallowing and trouble with saliva, without a scope.
a.x: Mrs. Ola should have had a neck X-ray and a scope by ENT to find and remove the bone.
a.w: A bone stuck low in the throat can make a hole in the gullet and cause a serious infection. Pain on swallowing and trouble with saliva suggest it is still there.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed checked her tonsils.
a.x: The tonsils were irrelevant.
a.w: Fish bones often stick in the tonsils.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed explained that a scratch can feel like a stuck bone.
a.x: That was misleading.
a.w: A scratch often feels like a bone; it was the low position and saliva trouble that needed checking.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave painkillers.
a.x: She should not have had painkillers.
a.w: Painkillers help her swallow.

s:
Laila, 2, woke up at night with a barking cough and a hoarse voice. She had a cold for two days. Her parents brought her in because she was making a harsh noise when breathing in, even while sitting quietly.

Dr. Tamer found her alert, with a temperature of 38°C. She had a noisy breath at rest and mild pulling in at the bottom of her neck. Her oxygen was 96 percent. She was drinking.

He explained that this was croup, a viral infection of the voice box. He told the parents to keep her calm and avoid upsetting her.

He advised them to sit in a steamy bathroom with her at home, saying "steam is the best treatment". He sent them home without any medicine.
h: He advised them to sit in a steamy bathroom with her at home, saying "steam is the best treatment"

a.o: Dr. Tamer sent home a toddler with croup and noise at rest without a dose of dexamethasone.
a.x: Laila should have had a single dose of oral dexamethasone, and been watched before going home.
a.w: Steroids reduce swelling in croup and lower the chance of needing hospital care. Steam has not been shown to help.

a.o: Dr. Tamer told them to keep her calm.
a.x: Calm doesn't matter.
a.w: Crying makes croup worse, so keeping a child calm helps.

a.o: Dr. Tamer checked her oxygen.
a.x: Oxygen checks were unnecessary.
a.w: Low oxygen is a sign of severe croup.

a.o: Dr. Tamer explained that croup is viral.
a.x: He should have said it was bacterial.
a.w: Croup is usually caused by viruses.

t: Hearing loss in a baby missed
s:
Baby Salma, 9 months old, came in for a routine check. Her mother said she smiled and played but did not turn to her name or loud noises. She did not babble like her older brother had. She was born early, at 32 weeks, and spent three weeks in the neonatal unit with an infection treated with gentamicin.

Dr. Rehab found a happy baby who was sitting and reaching for toys. Her ears looked normal.

She explained that babies develop at different speeds, especially premature babies. She told the mother to talk to Salma a lot.

She asked the mother to come back in six months to see if Salma started talking. She did not arrange a hearing test, saying "her newborn screening must have been normal". The mother wasn't sure whether the screening was done.
h: She did not arrange a hearing test, saying "her newborn screening must have been normal"

a.o: Dr. Rehab did not arrange a hearing test for a baby who doesn't react to sounds and had risk factors.
a.x: Salma should have had an urgent hearing test.
a.w: Premature babies who had gentamicin are at high risk of hearing loss. Not turning to sounds or babbling at 9 months needs testing now.

a.o: Dr. Rehab said babies develop at different speeds.
a.x: That was false reassurance.
a.w: Babies do vary, but warning signs still need checking.

a.o: Dr. Rehab told the mother to talk to Salma a lot.
a.x: Talking doesn't help.
a.w: Talking to babies supports language.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Salma's sitting and reaching.
a.x: Movement was irrelevant.
a.w: Checking all development helps see if a delay is only in hearing.

s:
Mrs. Samira, 52, had her thyroid removed this morning for a large goiter. In the evening the nurse called Dr. Kareem because she was anxious and short of breath. Her neck was swelling under the dressing and she had a high-pitched noise when breathing in.

Her oxygen was 92 percent and her pulse 118. Her voice was weak. The neck wound looked tense and swollen. She had been given a blood thinner injection for clot prevention in the afternoon.

Dr. Kareem gave oxygen and nebulized adrenaline and called the surgeon and the anesthetist. He asked for blood tests including calcium.

While waiting, he left the stitches in and the dressing on, writing "await surgeon to assess". The swelling kept growing and her breathing got noisier.
h: he left the stitches in and the dressing on, writing "await surgeon to assess"

a.o: Dr. Kareem left the stitches in a swelling neck wound with stridor after thyroid surgery.
a.x: The dressing and stitches should have been opened at once at the bedside to release the blood clot.
a.w: Bleeding under a thyroid wound can squash the windpipe within minutes. Opening the wound to let the clot out saves life.

a.o: Dr. Kareem checked her calcium.
a.x: Calcium was not relevant.
a.w: Low calcium is a common problem after thyroid surgery.

a.o: Dr. Kareem called the anesthetist.
a.x: The anesthetist was not needed.
a.w: Airway problems need an anesthetist.

a.o: Dr. Kareem gave nebulized adrenaline.
a.x: Adrenaline was useless.
a.w: It can briefly reduce swelling while help comes.

s:
Mr. Raafat, 60, came in about a white patch on the side of his tongue for four months. It did not wipe off and was not painful. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and chews tobacco. He drinks alcohol most evenings.

Dr. Inas found a 1.5 cm white patch with a slightly rough surface on the left side of his tongue. There were no neck lumps. His teeth were in poor condition.

She explained that this could be leukoplakia, a white patch that sometimes turns into cancer. She advised better dental care and booked a dentist appointment.

She told him to rinse with an antifungal mouthwash for two weeks and come back if it didn't go. She did not take a biopsy or mention stopping smoking and chewing tobacco.
h: She did not take a biopsy or mention stopping smoking and chewing tobacco

a.o: Dr. Inas did not biopsy a white tongue patch in a heavy smoker or tell him to stop tobacco.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have had a biopsy and strong advice and help to stop smoking, chewing tobacco and drinking.
a.w: Leukoplakia can be pre-cancer, especially in smokers and drinkers. A biopsy shows the risk, and stopping tobacco is the most important step.

a.o: Dr. Inas booked a dentist appointment.
a.x: Teeth were irrelevant.
a.w: Poor teeth can rub the tongue and keep it irritated.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked for neck lumps.
a.x: Neck lumps were irrelevant.
a.w: Neck lumps could mean spread of cancer.

t: Tinnitus in one ear not scanned
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 47, came in with ringing in her left ear for six months. She also felt she heard less on the left and had slight unsteadiness. Her right ear was fine. She has no history of loud noise exposure.

Dr. Fouad found both eardrums normal. Her hearing test showed a nerve hearing loss in the left ear only. Her facial movement and feeling were normal. She works as an accountant and finds the ringing worst at night when the office is quiet. She drinks two coffees a day and takes no regular medicines.

He explained that ringing in the ears is very common and usually harmless. He suggested background noise at night and relaxation exercises.

He told her she could live with it and booked no further tests, writing "tinnitus, reassured".
h: booked no further tests, writing "tinnitus, reassured"

a.o: Dr. Fouad did not order an MRI for one-sided ringing with one-sided nerve hearing loss and unsteadiness.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had an MRI to look for a growth on the hearing nerve.
a.w: Ringing and hearing loss in one ear can be caused by an acoustic neuroma. It needs an MRI.

a.o: Dr. Fouad suggested background noise at night.
a.x: That makes tinnitus worse.
a.w: Background sound can help mask the ringing.

a.o: Dr. Fouad checked her facial movement.
a.x: The face is not related.
a.w: A growth on the nerve can press on the facial nerve.

a.o: Dr. Fouad did a hearing test.
a.x: The hearing test was pointless.
a.w: It showed the one-sided loss, which is important.

s:
It was almost five in the afternoon when Mr. Tarek rushed into the ER carrying his nephew Omar, a skinny nine-year-old with a towel pressed to his left arm. Omar had crashed his bicycle into broken glass outside the bakery. By the time they arrived the bleeding had stopped, but the towel was soaked and Omar was pale and crying.

Nurse Salma checked him quickly. His heart was racing at 112, but his blood pressure was fine and he was talking clearly, so she put him in the yellow area. Omar weighed 28 kg, had no allergies his uncle knew of, and had his last tetanus shot at six.

Dr. Hany unwrapped the towel and found a clean 5 cm cut on the inside of the forearm. Omar could move every finger. "We'll need stitches," Dr. Hany said. Mr. Tarek nodded. "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him." Dr. Hany washed the wound, numbed it with lidocaine and closed it with six neat stitches. He gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol for the pain and sent him home with his uncle and a wound-care leaflet.
h: "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him."

a.o: Dr. Hany stitched Omar's arm after only his uncle agreed, when his parents were a phone call away.
a.x: Dr. Hany should have phoned Omar's parents for consent before stitching.
a.w: An uncle is not Omar's legal guardian. The bleeding had stopped, so this was not an emergency and there was time to reach a parent.

a.o: Nurse Salma sent Omar to the yellow area, when a child cut by glass with a racing heart should be seen first.
a.x: Omar should have gone straight to the red area.
a.w: Yellow was right: the bleeding had stopped, his blood pressure was normal and he was talking. A fast heart in a scared, crying child is not shock.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol, far too much for a 28 kg boy.
a.x: Omar should have had 280 mg of paracetamol.
a.w: 420 mg is 15 mg/kg for a 28 kg child, a normal dose.

a.o: Omar went home without a tetanus shot after falling on dirty glass.
a.x: Omar should have had a tetanus booster before leaving.
a.w: His last tetanus shot was three years ago. A dirty wound needs a booster only if the last one was more than 5 years ago.
